articles.title: Porth woman died from cancer after nine-month wait for test results
articles.summary: Sarah Catherine Daniels did not receive potentially life-extending treatment fast enough, an inquest heard.
articles.body:
A mum-of-three died from cancer following a nine-month delay in receiving pathology test results, meaning she did not receive potentially life-extending treatment fast enough, an inquest has heard.

Sarah Catherine Daniels' husband said she "never gave up" trying to fight her rare and aggressive cancer, but died at home in Porth, Rhondda Cynon Taf, aged 43 in April 2025.

Coroner Rachel Knight said the pathology department where a mass from Sarah's ovary had been sent for testing was at the time "completely overwhelmed by demand" following the Covid-19 pandemic.

She told the inquest at Pontypridd Coroners' Court that the delay was "unacceptable" and reduced the chance of successful chemotherapy.

Sarah first presented to her GP aged 39 in October 2021 with "gynaecological symptoms of concern", the inquest was told on Monday.

The matter was escalated by her doctor, resulting in an ultrasound scan on 21 October in 2021 which identified a mass on one of her ovaries. Sarah was then referred to gynaecology in the Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board area.

She was given two surgical options, which included a total hysterectomy or a less invasive procedure to remove the mass.

The full hysterectomy would have triggered an early menopause as well as other effects, so the inquest was told that Sarah opted for the less invasive procedure.

In February 2022 the mass was removed, which did not have the expected appearance of a cancer, but samples were sent to pathology for testing.

Giving evidence, Martin Ludlam, a biomedical scientist who worked as the cellular pathology and mortuary service manager at the health board, said the situation at the time was difficult.

He said that during late 2021 and 2022 their workload significantly increased due to many routine appointments being put on hold during the Covid-19 pandemic.

He said they had an insufficient capacity to manage the current demand as well as the backlog.

Ludlam told the inquest that by the end of 2022 the health board was no longer dealing with a backlog in part due to outsourcing, which he said they were still using today.

"This case has highlighted the case that we can never go back to a position where we have a routine backlog again," he said.

Ben Daniels, Sarah's husband, gave written evidence and said when Sarah received her results she was told that her condition was terminal and that her life expectancy was 12 months.

He described how his wife was determined to get better and sought private treatment at the Christie cancer treatment centre in Manchester, which included the removal of her appendix.

Sarah then received follow up treatment at Velindre Cancer Centre in Cardiff which included 10 rounds of chemotherapy and scans.

She got the all clear, but some months later scans revealed that cancer was present.

This time Sarah struggled to have blood markers in the safe remit to receive regular chemotherapy, which meant treatment was "sporadic".

Ben said his wife "never gave up" trying to fight her illness but by January 2025 her health had gotten "progressively worse".

Dr Kein Yim, a consultant in clinical oncology at Velindre said that in March 2025 it was clear that her condition was declining and a decision was made that she was too frail for any more chemotherapy.

Sarah died at home in Porth on 15 April 2025, surrounded by loved ones.

Mohamed Khalifa, a consultant in obstetrics and gynaecology who leads gynaecological cancer multidisciplinary team (MDT) meetings for the Cwm Taf health board, gave evidence about the significance of the nine month pathology delay in Sarah's case.

He said that Sarah had lost time in her cancer treatment due to the delay between surgery and histology. He also said her Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) had been "incorrectly reassuring" to her and her family.

"When she died might have been different if the chemotherapy or other treatment had been started sooner. The delay of [nine] months between surgery and histology was unacceptable," he said.

Knight told the inquest that initial aspects of Sarah's care were dealt with in appropriate time, including her initial GP referral and her MRI scan on November 10.

The coroner said there was "low suspicion" that Sarah had cancer at that stage and that it was "reasonable" that medics did not seek an MRI scan of a wider area like her entire abdomen which may have revealed her appendix cancer.

She said evidence corroborated that the mass did not have the appearance of cancer, and that samples were sent "appropriately" to pathology for testing.

However, she noted that the pathology department was "completely overwhelmed by demand" due to pre and post-Covid factors including staffing and a huge backlog.

Drawing on evidence she stated that the department had begun outsourcing its backlog, but that this was in its infancy. At present she said there had been no "overhaul" of the system, but that a better framework had been established by the health board.

She said she found the nine month delay between Sarah's surgery and result "unacceptable", and noted that the issue was accepted by the health board. She said that Sarah had been living with stage four cancer since October 2021, and that the delay likely impacted her treatment as well as her quality and length of life.

She said the delay reduced the chance of success in cancer control through chemotherapy.

Sarah's medical cause of death was recorded as "metastatic signet ring adenocarcinoma of the appendix".

Although Knight noted that the medical cause of death was "naturally occurring", she opted for a narrative conclusion to reflect the full circumstances of Sarah's death.

Knight apologised to Ben and their children: "I'm sorry you lost Sarah in the way you did. You have shown great dignity throughout the proceedings... What you went though must have been horrendous."

She added it is clear "how loved Sarah was and how missed she is".

articles.title: Zoos help to save snail found in only one lake in Wales
articles.summary: Once prevalent across the UK, this mollusc is now only found in one lake in Wales.
articles.body:
A tiny snail found in only one lake in the UK has been dubbed as precious as an Egyptian artefact as conservationists bid to save it.

Several British zoos are setting up so-called ark populations of the glutinous snail, one of Europe's rarest species, using creatures bred in a back garden in Ceredigion.

"Beguiled by their cuteness," conservationist Ian Hughes has made it his "life-defining" mission to protect the threatened mollusc, which was once widespread in UK waters.

"There was a point where we'd got more snails in our garden than have ever been seen in the wild," he said.

Myxas glutinosa gets its name from the gooey mantle that covers its extremely delicate, gold-flecked brown shell.

It is no bigger than a fingertip, but has comically large antennae - which Hughes likens to "big floppy ears".

The snails, which feed on algae and are considered an indicator of healthy lakes and rivers, have been driven to extinction across England.

Polluted water and habitat loss are largely blamed for their disappearance.

Hughes said the snails were "something to preserve and cherish like Egyptian artefacts".

In the UK, their last known refuge is Wales' largest natural lake - Llyn Tegid - in Eryri National Park, also known as Snowdonia.

Since 2014, under licence from Natural Resources Wales, Hughes has been wading into the lake to collect and study the snails.

He has designed and installed small concrete shelters for them in the lake itself, and set up his own captive population in a greenhouse at his home in Llanarth.

Hughes was left wondering "will they survive an hour, will they survive a day"?

Then, after four months, eggs were spotted in the tank.

"Nobody had knowingly seen their eggs before we made that breakthrough," he said.

"You do these things on a wing and a prayer when you're trying to save something that's down to a single site and you're trying to fathom what it needs and how to save it.

"So when something actually works - it's one of those life-defining moments."

Rearing the snails - as well as other critically endangered invertebrates such as scarlet malachite beetles, ladybird spiders and tadpole shrimp - has become a family affair.

Ian's wife Kerry and their sons Jake, George and Ben, are also fully invested.

"You've got to have a certain mindset to walk out into a freezing cold lake in the middle of January," Ben, 27, explained.

"But knowing that you're helping is more than enough to make it all worth it.

"Every little thing has its place in the ecosystem and if you take a tiny little cog out of any machine it's going to stop working".

The Hughes family is now working with the British and Irish Association of Zoos and Aquariums (BIAZA) to relocate some of their snails to wildlife parks across England.

It is seen as a first step towards restoring them back to locations in the wild over the coming years, as part of a £60m UK government-backed scheme to protect rare species.

"It's such a hugely important conservation project and such a wonderful story," explained Samantha Eden, assistant curator at Wingham Wildlife Park in Kent, who travelled to the Hughes home to pick up 24 glutinous snails.

"We've got a new facility that we've set up for them - three beautiful ponds where we're going to be breeding them, learning about them and understanding a little bit more about their environmental needs."

Askham Bryan Wildlife Park in York and Longleat in Wiltshire, along with Dudley and Chester zoos are also taking part in the project, with the Freshwater Habitats Trust searching for suitable water bodies where the snails could eventually be released.

"We're doing a lot of research on the snails' ecology, their husbandry and their genetics," explained Nicky Needham, head of species management and conservation at BIAZA.

"If we can build up a really strong picture then we're in a good position to reintroduce some of them [to the wild].

"With fingers and toes crossed I'd like to think that we could achieve that within three years' time."

"I think it's an amazing project and we'll support it as much as we can," said Simon Jones, assistant warden at Eryri National Park, who added the park was "really proud" to be home to the "unique species".

But climate change means these species are "at an increased threat" and, with the zoos' help, "there's more of a chance of keeping the population alive".

For Hughes, it is "very exciting" so see fresh momentum behind saving the glutinous snail.

"Having all your eggs in one basket is always a dangerous move so having more experts looking after it is really the right way to go," he said.

"For me they're an absolute treasure - like an Egyptian artefact... as valuable as that," he added - "and preserving them is a duty to our children and grandchildren".

articles.title: UK man pleads guilty to using online forum to encourage sexual assault of unconscious women
articles.summary: A man from North London pleaded guilty to charges related to encouraging other members of an online forum to sexually assault drugged victims, London’s Metropolitan Police announced on Friday.
articles.body: A man from North London pleaded guilty to charges related to encouraging other members of an online forum to sexually assault drugged victims, London’s Metropolitan Police announced on Friday. Police discovered the forum in October 2025 and established a national coordination group, led by the UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA), to investigate the matter. The investigation led authorities to 52-year-old Darren Conway of Enfield, whom officers had identified as one of the group chat members. On July 30, police executed a search warrant on Conway’s home, where they seized his digital devices and arrested him. Messages on his devices revealed that Conway had urged other forum members to engage in sexual assault against drugged or sleeping women, later encouraging the perpetrators to share images in the chat, according to Met Police. Through the chat room, Conway viewed sleeping women more than 10 times, police said. “Conway’s actions were shocking. By encouraging others to engage in sexual offending against victims who were unconscious, asleep, or otherwise stupefied, he has put women at a serious risk of harm in their own homes — all for his own sexual gratification,” Met Police Commander Andy Day said. On Friday, Conway appeared in London’s Wood Green Crown Court and pleaded guilty to nine counts of assisting or encouraging an offense, in addition to charges of voyeurism and possessing an extreme pornographic image. In court, Conway wore a gray tracksuit and spoke only to confirm his name and to plead guilty, the UK’s Press Association (PA). reported. He is set to be charged on October 30. ‘Vile acts against women’ The case is representative of a wider trend of online forums serving as platforms for offenders to encourage others to drug and sexually assault unconscious victims. An international police operation uncovered a highly organized online ecosystem of offenders, Europol and Britain’s NCA revealed in July. In the chatrooms, the predominantly male perpetrators coordinate assaults and share information and imagery of the abuse, authorities said. Ciara Bergman, the CEO of Rape Crisis England & Wales – a charity that provides services to people affected by sexual violence and abuse – said that the scale and coordination of the drug-facilitated sexual abuse on the forums was “deeply alarming.” “Sadly, though, they are not surprising,” Bergman added. “These abuses are rooted in the same misogyny and objectification which underpin violence against women and girls the world over.” CNN conducted an undercover investigation into the issue, discovering online networks in which men encourage others to commit sexually violent acts against women. The issue was brought to a global audience during the high-profile case of Gisele Pelicot in France. Pelicot’s former husband was sentenced to 20 years in prison after he solicited dozens of strangers to rape his then-wife while she was unconscious. The shocking crime ignited conversations around the presence of gender-based violence in France. Since then, police have made several arrests and secured convictions in similar cases across Europe. In many instances, the victims are unaware that they have been sexually assaulted until they are contacted by police, the NCA said. Following Conway’s guilty plea, officers are continuing to work on identifying the individuals seen in the footage recovered from his seized devices. Many of the victims are believed to reside in the UK, but some may live overseas, according to Met Police. The chief prosecutor in the case, Tracy Easton, said that Conway had committed “vile acts against women in their own homes.” “Organized drug-facilitated sexual assault is abhorrent and we are determined to work with policing to bring offenders to justice,” Easton said. “I hope this guilty plea gives confidence to anyone who believes they may have been subjected to similar abuse to come forward.”

articles.title: Israeli demolitions threaten schools and homes in Masafer Yatta
articles.summary: Students pledge to continue learning as Masafer Yatta demolitions target homes, schools, and their right to education.
articles.body:
On Tuesday morning, 12-year-old Sundus al-Hamamdeh left her home in the Masafer Yatta village of Khirbet al-Fakhit, and went to school.

It was the third day of the new school year in the occupied West Bank.

But when the sixth-grade student at al-Fakhit Secondary School returned from her classes, the house she had left behind was gone.

Israeli forces had carried out a large-scale demolition operation in Khirbet al-Fakhit, destroying homes, livestock shelters, water infrastructure, and solar-power installations.

For al-Hamamdeh, her house was more than four walls and a roof. It was her safe space, the place she came back to every day.

For children in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron in the occupied West Bank, the spectre of demolition is always present.

Much of Masafer Yatta lies in Area C of the West Bank, where Israel has control over planning and construction. Israeli authorities justifies the demolition orders by saying that the structures were built without permits; Palestinians, backed by the United Nations, note that such permits are nearly impossible for them to obtain.

And it’s not just their homes that are under threat, but their schools.

On August 4, Israeli forces surrounded Shaab al-Butum school , according to Bassam Jabr, the director-general of education in Masafer Yatta.

An Israeli military bulldozer then demolished two rooms used by teachers and administrators, and a storage room.

The UN independently documented the demolition of the rooms, saying Israeli authorities had cited the lack of an Israeli-issued building permit.

Things could still get worse; the main school building remains under a demolition order.

Established in 2015, the school serves about 60 students from kindergarten through 11th grade. Its remote location makes transferring students to other schools particularly difficult, Jabr said.

Education officials have appealed to Israeli courts, and called on the United Nations and foreign governments to intervene.

But the schools remain under threat. Even as the Israeli military and settlers’ pogroms against Palestinians continue across the West Bank, Masafer Yatta is especially targeted.

The remote communities there have little ability to defend themselves and conditions are harsh. In addition, the Israeli military has designated large parts of the area a military firing zone, another justification for forcing out the Palestinian population.

Masafer Yatta’s schools are a central part of the effort to keep Palestinians here – ensuring that families do not have to travel far for their children to be educated. Palestinians argue that is why the schools have been particularly targeted.

Intisar Omar Abu Sabha, an administrative director at the Masafer Yatta Directorate of Education, says schools in the communities of Zif, ar-Rifaiyah, Umm Qussa, Umm al-Kheir, Jinba, Shaab al-Butum, Khirbet al-Daba, and al-Majaz are among those facing demolition orders.

In addition to the threats to their schools, students and teachers also have to navigate road closures, checkpoints, and the presence of settlers to reach their classrooms.

Abu Sabha said schools have also faced damage and settler incursions or harassment in and around their grounds. She describes a cycle in which children risk losing both their homes and their schools.

“Imagine a student who is at school, then returns home and finds their home demolished … and comes back the next day to find their school demolished,” she said.

Yasmeen Sallaq, a Palestinian lawyer, says the threat to the Masafer Yatta schools directly undermines children’s right to education.

But Sallaq says that Israeli restrictions on movement, military raids, arrests, displacement, and attacks affecting students and education workers make that right increasingly difficult to exercise.

“We face the demolition of schools every day, making the continuation of the educational process almost impossible,” Sallaq said.

At Zif Secondary School for Girls , headteacher Hanaa al-Salameen says about 250 students attend the school.

It first received a demolition notice in 2016. Years of legal proceedings followed, but an appeal against demolition was dismissed this year, with efforts continuing to obtain an interim injunction.

The uncertainty has already taken a toll. Some girls are experiencing fear and anxiety, while others have transferred to different schools, al-Salameen said.

“The school is not just a place for education,” she said. “This school is the students’ only outlet.”

She fears the school’s demolition could push some girls out of education altogether if alternative schools are too far away or require them to travel along unsafe roads.

At Zif, 10th-grade student Rabiha Yousef Jibril described the school’s importance.

“I am growing up in this school, and my dreams are growing with me day by day,” Jibril said, adding that while students fear its demolition, they insist they will continue to attend.

“Even if they demolish the school, we will continue to study, even under the trees,” she said. “Even if they confiscate the books, we will keep them in our hearts, as well as our minds.”

articles.title: 40% of global GDP is here: PM Modi
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Noting that the Brics grouping now represents 50% of the global population, 40% of GDP, and 25% of trade, PM Narendra Modi said Friday that.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Noting that the Brics grouping now represents 50% of the global population, 40% of GDP, and 25% of trade, PM Narendra Modi said Friday that their collective economic might has grown at nearly double the global pace since the bloc was formed in 2006, and called upon member countries to reduce barriers to trade and increase opportunities for businesses.In his address at the Brics Business Forum, PM also underlined the need to keep trade flowing. "Global trade can move forward only when sea lanes are secure, supply routes are open, and seafarers are safe. And, therefore, Bharat is a firm supporter of freedom of navigation and the safety of seafarers," Modi said, his remark coming against the backdrop of disruption of traffic through Strait of Hormuz and the growing threat through Bab al-Mandab Strait, another crucial artery for India.His pitch for deeper engagement significantly contrasted the themes of 2 other key members: Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.Putin, like PM, also invoked the growing economic heft of Brics members. However, he and Pezeshkian, with their countries reeling from sanctions, were resentful of the West's continuing sway."The world is changing... Over the past 5 years, as it has been said today - I think it was our Indonesian colleague who said it, the Brics countries accounted for over 40% of global GDP, while the contribution of Group of Seven, the so-called leading economies, although I don't understand why they are called 'leading', was just 29%," Putin said.PM Modi's 'Intra-Brics trade' call seen as aimed at US and ChinaAt a time when trade barriers are increasing, India is building economic bridges, PM Narendra Modi said, adding, “Our approach in Brics is also the same: to reduce barriers and increase opportunities for businesses.”He has been averse to Brics being turned into an anti-West bloc and has resisted the push from China, Russia and Iran for de-dollarisation. Also, his call for greater intra-Brics commerce can be seen as aimed at both US President Trump’s strong arm tariff tactics as well as a reminder of New Delhi’s contention to China that it needed to let in more Indian goods and should not weaponise supplies of equipment and raw materials needed by Indian manufacturers.“In these years, the combined GDP of Brics countries has grown by about 4.5 times while the global GDP has grown by around 2.5 times. Brics’s economic strength has grown at nearly double the pace of the world,” Modi said, pointing to the bloc comprising emerging markets and developing economies.He called upon the Brics Business Council to identify the top 10 trade barriers to be removed, while charting the growth trajectory of the Indian economy in the last 12 years since his govt took office with its focus on innovation and resilience.“Can we support 100 Brics startups every year to scale in other Brics markets? Can we develop 1,000 new partnerships among our businesses? On all these benchmarks, we have to review our progress every year. Let us turn the ambition of Brics into action and its collective strength into global solutions. Let Brics move forward and take the world forward as well.”Lauding Brics nations for becoming key centres for global innovation and solutions — from grassroots to frontier tech — he said the bloc’s growing scale, speed, and optimism are clearly visible.With the theme of India’s Brics presidency being “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Co-operation and Sustainability”, he said India has made this foundation of its economic and trade policy.India has made supply chains from energy to technology more diversified and reliable, he said, adding that it is offering confidence in growth and stability even amid global uncertainties.“We are rapidly expanding roads, railways, ports, and airports. Along with this, we are building new capabilities in strategic sectors such as ship-building, semiconductor, quantum, critical minerals, and bio-tech,” he said.Turning to his govt’s call to the global business for “Make in India, Innovate with India, Scale for the World”, he said the country has more than two lakh start-ups, and over 120 unicorns, which are transforming education and healthcare through AI, crossing new frontiers in defence and space, and working on green hydrogen and batteries as well.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: Robert De Niro called Zohran Mamdani's defund the police comments "ridiculous" but argued the NYC mayor should still attend the 9/11 memorial.
articles.body: Outspoken liberal actor Robert De Niro agreed with some of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s critics that his comments on law enforcement were "ridiculous" but still argued the mayor should attend Friday’s 9/11 memorial. Political rancor has threatened to cast a long shadow over this year's Sept. 11 remembrance events, marking 25 years since the tragedy that rocked the United States. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's past rhetoric and links to terror sympathizers are spurring intense backlash ahead of the city's events memorializing the World Trade Center attacks, with Republicans and people whose lives were changed by the attacks demanding he not attend. The Hollywood Reporter noted the controversy when it spoke to De Niro in an interview published Thursday, asking, "Do you think he should be there?" "I don’t see why he shouldn’t come," De Niro said. "He’s the mayor. I haven’t heard him say or do anything yet that would disqualify him from being there. Maybe I’m naive, but you have to give the guy a chance. He’s not a part of what happened." MAMDANI HEADS TO 9/11 MEMORIAL DESPITE 110,000-SIGNATURE PUSH FROM VICTIMS’ FAMILIES TO STAY AWAY One of the past comments Mamdani has been grilled about repeatedly is his criticism of the NYPD amid the George Floyd riots of 2020. Mamdani called to "defund the police" in 2020 and labeled the NYPD "racist, anti-queer and a major threat to public safety." When De Niro was asked further about whether he could understand why some families would find it problematic, he paused for a moment and answered, "I understand their pain, but I still think he should be there. "I think this stems from tension he’s had with the fire department and the comments about defund the police, which I don’t think he really meant," the interviewer added. "Well he did say it. And, of course, it’s ridiculous," De Niro said. "You can’t defund the police. It’s not going to happen. But I still think he should be at the memorial." He went on to suggest Mamdani could use the opportunity "as a bridge" to unite people. When asked about President Donald Trump, however, De Niro offered a far sharper reply, saying, "We have to stop him. It’s insane. We have to send people to voting booths and make sure they can go in. Just watch to keep them safe. It’s crazy we’re here, but this is where we are. We have to protect our elections." Entertainment commentator Christian Toto responded to the actor’s interview. "The Hollywood Reporter eggs on Robert De Niro, sans fact checking, because it agrees with most of what he says. The outlet understands the actor's lack of information on key political subjects, too, but it cheers him on because he's anti-Trump and anti-GOP," Toto told Fox News Digital. "Meanwhile, the actor hasn't a clue about the mayor's past comments, his toxic associations or why his 'defund the police' beliefs are so damaging. He's a useful idiot for the left, and The Hollywood Reporter is all too happy to magnify his idiocy." 9/11 FAMILIES PUSH TO BAN MAMDANI FROM 25TH ANNIVERSARY REMEMBRANCE OVER 'HOSTILE' RECORD An online petition led by family members of people killed on Sept. 11 — signed by over 100,000 people — called on Mamdani to skip the memorial. "Mr. Mamdani has praised Brooklyn Imam Siraj Wahhaj, who has been linked to radical Islam, was named as an alleged co-conspirator in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing and served as a character witness for the 'Blind Sheikh,' who was convicted in 1995 of plotting terror attacks against the United States," the petition said. "Mr. Mamdani has endorsed candidates such as Aber Kawas, who described 9/11 as an attack 'a couple of people did in the context of U.S. capitalism, racism, White supremacy, and Islamophobia,' and who also expressed sympathy for Ahmed Ferhani, who pleaded guilty to plotting to blow up a Manhattan synagogue." Mamdani and other socialist candidates' associated with far-left activist Hasan Piker have also gotten intense scrutiny over Piker's past comments that the United States "deserved" the attacks, remarks he promptly walked back at the time but continue to haunt him and his political circle. Mamdani has also condemned the comment. Mamdani has faced backlash for giving a ceremonial pen from a 9/11 remembrance ceremony to a top aide who once represented a convicted al Qaeda member. Mamdani handed the pen to his chief counsel, Ramzi Kassem. Kassem previously represented Ahmed al-Darbi, who pleaded guilty to war crime charges tied to al Qaeda plots against commercial ships and was the brother-in-law of Khalid al-Mihdhar, one of the hijackers aboard American Airlines Flight 77, which crashed into the Pentagon, killing 184. Rafael Mangual, the head of research for the Manhattan Institute’s Policing & Public Safety Initiative, argued that De Niro and the interviewer sorely missed the mark in recalling Mamdani's record. "I’m not sure I share Mr. DeNiro’s dismissal of calls for Mayor Mamdani to keep away from the official memorial ceremony at the site of the World Trade Center on Friday," he said. "Nor do I think the mayor’s past expressions of vitriol for the NYPD — whose members bravely ran to the assistance of their fellow Americans that tragic morning 25 years ago — are the only justifications for the anger of the families that have expressed their preference for the mayor not to attend Friday’s ceremony." "As a rapper, Mamdani praised the Holy Land Five, a group convicted of providing material support to Hamas, an Islamist terrorist organization," Mangual continued. "On the mayoral campaign trail, Mamdani posed for a photo op with Siraj Wahaj, an unindicted co-conspirator in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing who also testified as a character witness on behalf of Sheikh Omar Abdel-Rahman, who had lectured at Wahaj’s mosque prior to being convicted of several terrorism charges in the mid-1990s. "During his campaign, he also paled around with Hasan Piker, who stated that America deserved 9/11 and praised the mujahideen for shooting and wounding then-Navy SEAL and current Congressman Dan Crenshaw," he added. "And as mayor, Mamdani hired as his chief legal counsel Ramzi Kassem, who volunteered to represent pro bono a Guantánamo Bay detainee and convicted al Qaeda terrorist Ahmed al-Darbi. When coupled with his vitriolic criticisms of the very institutions tasked with keeping us safe from terrorist threats, the wishes of the families De Niro was asked about become much harder to ignore." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Mary Marslender, a former Trump appointee and senior advisor to the U.S. Senate and now a Republican consultant, argued that Mamdani cannot outrun his past call to defund the police so easily. "Mamdani has spent years portraying New York’s brave first responders as the problem, and Robert De Niro knows that. Mamdani ran for mayor on a platform of defunding the police, only walking back his stance for political gain — not out of genuine conviction," she said. "He has also refused to distance himself from extremist voices who blame America for 9/11 and declined to condemn the phrase 'globalize the intifada,' claiming he won’t police language," Marslender added. "Robert De Niro’s defense of Mamdani’s views reflects a troubling disregard for the values that unite Americans." Former RNC national spokesperson Elizabeth Pipko argued that De Niro has a long pattern of clumsy political commentary. "Robert De Niro is again showing his privilege and ignorance," she said. "He has decided because he aligns politically with Mamdani, he will defend him without knowing the facts. Similarly, he will attack Trump, even when discussing 9/11, because he dislikes him, again without knowing any facts." "Mamdani has said horrific things about the NYPD and those who protect our great country. Yes, but unfortunately, he has also praised a man that was named by federal prosecutors as a co-conspirator in connection with the 1993 World Trade Center bombing case," Marslender continued. "He campaigns with Hasan Piker, who has a framed photo of the Twin Towers burning standing on his desk. He refuses to condemn the phrase 'globalize the intifada.' Ironically, that phrase is exactly what 9/11 was about. "Just once, I’d like to see De Niro confronted with these facts and the sad reality of his own ignorance," she said. "I’d be curious what his excuses would be then." Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani’s office for comment but did not immediately receive a response. articles.title: Man arrested in connection with death of Tasia Fortune in Mississippi
articles.summary: A man has been arrested in the death of Tasia Fortune, the 29-year-old Black woman who was found hanging from a tree in Mississippi last month, police announced Friday.
articles.body: A man has been arrested in the death of Tasia Fortune, the 29-year-old Black woman who was found hanging from a tree in Mississippi last month, police announced Friday. Jacques Ratliff was arrested Friday afternoon and will be charged with homicide, Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney told reporters. She said he had an “association” with Fortune, but did not disclose what kind. Fortune’s body was discovered Aug. 3 behind an abandoned building in Jackson. Her family had previously said they did not believe Fortune died by suicide. The case sparked widespread alarm and media attention given Mississippi’s sordid history with racial violence. Her death was officially classified as a homicide Thursday evening, Brackney said. That determination led police to secure two search warrants and an arrest warrant for Ratliff, she said. Investigators served the search warrants Friday, but Ratliff was not found at the location. Officers heading back to headquarters later found him walking along Capitol Street and took him into custody, Brackney said. “The arrest today is an important development in this investigation, but it is not the conclusion. This case remains active, and additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence wherever it leads,” she said, adding: “because Tasia and her children deserve nothing less.” It’s not immediately clear whether Ratliff has retained an attorney. Brackney said the Fortune family was immediately notified of the arrest. While Fortune’s death has been ruled a homicide, Brackney — who was cautious as she described Fortune as found “in a hanging position” — did not elaborate on the cause of death determination. The chief acknowledged the scrutiny into the case, saying, “We understand the questions and the desire for answers given Mississippi’s history,” but stressed the case must be based on evidence and facts.

articles.title: WWE's Rey Mysterio reflects on Triplemania involvement, says he's unfazed going into match with 7-foot-3 giant
articles.summary: Rey Mysterio faces the 7-foot-3 Omos in the Triplemania 34 main event in Las Vegas, with Omos' AAA future hanging in the balance of the match.
articles.body: Before the 619 became a widely known finishing move, before Rey Mysterio became a WWE champion and the superstar he is today, he was getting his first opportunities in the ring at AAA. Mysterio took part in the first-ever Triplemania event in 1993. At the time, he was known as Rey Misterio Jr. and he teamed up with Volador and Misterioso to take on Tony Arce, Vulcano and Rocco Valente – known as Los Destructores. More than three decades later, AAA is a part of WWE, Mysterio is the general manager of AAA and he’s in the main event of Triplemania 34 Night 1 in Las Vegas. COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK "It’s a very special moment for me in so many ways," he told OutKick Dropkick. "The fact that I’m now the new GM of AAA. The fact that AAA was the first company that opened the doors for me and I was at the very first AAA show back in ’92. I was at the very first Triplemania in ’93. So, to see this come full circle and to be in the position where I’m at now, it’s been an amazing ride, man. "A lot of tasks at hand but I’ve been able to manage and control certain things to a certain extent. Obviously, things got out of control a little bit when I decided to jump on top of Omos and create this match we have tonight here for the first Triplemania in Las Vegas, which is also very special. We are, in the first time ever in the history of AAA, we’re doing a first-time, two-night Triplemania event. The one tonight here in Las Vegas and in two different countries and then Sunday in Mexico City." Mysterio’s rivalry with the 7-foot-3 giant Omos will seemingly come to an end on Friday night. He was forced to suspend Omos after he injured Galeno and attacked Mysterio in August. Omos showed up to Ola de Color as a paid spectator and attacked Mysterio again, with the help of Dominik Mysterio. Over the course of his career, Mysterio has slayed many beasts. He’s conquered mountains more than once. It’s why going up against Omos isn’t doing much to make him worried. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "I’ve felt his power. Very strong dude. Very intimidating," he said of Omos. "But it doesn’t faze me. I’ve seen giants before. I was just saying a minute ago, from the moment I started training at 8 years old, I was the smallest kid in the class. The youngest kid after me was probably 16, 17. They were obviously much bigger than me. I’ve always been in the ring with bigger people, bigger opponents, so, it doesn’t faze me. I’m not scared. I’m motivated. I’m antsy to step in the ring and I’m looking forward to tonight. "As a GM, I need to make a statement that no superstar or Luchador in the AAA locker room is going to try to intimidate me as the GM for AAA. And they have to know their boundaries and they have to not step over those boundaries and respect authority. In this case, this is what I had to do for Omos to respect some authority." If Mysterio loses, Omos will be reinstated to the AAA roster. Should he win, Omos will never be allowed to compete in AAA again. articles.title: Tasia Fortune: Arrest made over the death of black woman found hanged from tree
articles.summary: Tasia Fortune's body was found  in the lot of an abandoned home in Mississippi in August.
articles.body:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

Police in the US state of Mississippi have made their first arrest in the case of a black woman found dead and hanged from a tree, and say they could soon take more people into custody.

Tasia Fortune's body was found in the lot of an abandoned home in Jackson in August, but police only announced they were treating her death as a possible homicide earlier this week.

"That arrest today is an important development in this investigation, but it is not the conclusion," Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney said on Friday. "This case remains active."

Fortune's death has worried locals in Jackson, a majority-black city in a state with a history of racial violence and lynching.

During Friday's news conference, Brackney said the medical examiner had confirmed Fortune's cause of death was homicide, adding that a suspected killer would be charged with murder.

Police had arrested one man and "additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence", she said, adding that they had interviewed 15 people in the case.

Her mother, Christy Spivey, told the BBC that she cried when the police called to update her about the arrest, saying: "I guess I do feel like a little sigh of relief...like a little bit of peace just come over me."

"I just hope that they've got the right person," she added.

The arrest of a suspect followed weeks of what Spivey and residents in Jackson described as relative silence and inaction from local officials.

Combined with the grim nature of Fortune's death and Mississippi's history of racial lynchings, the lack of information about the case had left the community in shock and fear.

Spivey earlier told the BBC she had tried contacting Jackson police several times over the last two weeks, leaving multiple voicemails, and had not heard back.

Brackney addressed the family's frustration on Friday, saying: "We have been in constant contact with the mother and the stepfather, as well as the biological father, throughout this case."

A letter Spivey wrote to officials about the limited communication and speed of the investigation was read during a public city meeting on Tuesday - the same day Jackson police made the announcement about a possible homicide.

"I'm kind of like in awe," Spivey said. "Like, I can't believe it. That was quick."

Fortune's death has been described by a member of the US Congress as part of a pattern of "possible modern-day lynchings".

This week, more than 50 members of Congress sent a letter to the FBI and justice department, saying they were "extremely alarmed by reports of black people found hanging from trees in numerous states" and calling for an independent investigation into suspicious deaths of black Americans.

So far this year there have been at least 10 reported hangings of black people in the US, they said, adding that there were more than 70 lynchings documented between 2000 and 2025.

articles.title: Donald Trump: Protests expected as US President visits Ireland
articles.summary: Donald Trump will arrive on Saturday morning at Dublin Airport ahead of a two-day visit to Ireland.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump will arrive on Saturday morning at Dublin Airport ahead of a two-day visit to Ireland.

Trump will hold a courtesy call with Irish President Catherine Connolly as well as a bilateral meeting with Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin.

He will also attend events at the US Ambassador to Ireland Ed Walsh's residence in Dublin's Phoenix Park.

Trump will then attend the Amgen Irish Open golf tournament which is taking place at the Trump International Golf Links and Hotel Doonbeg in County Clare, which he owns.

He last visited the Republic in 2019, where he also spent time at his golf course.

Irish authorities have been planning for Trump's visit for months in what will be one of the biggest security operations in the history of the state.

Thousands of people are expected at protests in Dublin and a protest will also be held in Doonbeg.

His sons Eric and Donald Trump Junior are expected to accompany Trump in Doonbeg.

"We will have discussions with the president and there will be a reception in the American Embassy but I think he's also very anxious to get to Doonbeg and watch the Irish Open," Martin told the BBC's Borderlands podcast this week.

In a statement issued on Friday night in advance of Trump's arrival, Martin said:

"I look forward to welcoming President Trump to Ireland and to discussing the many issues of mutual interest and reaffirming the strong economic, cultural and people-to-people ties between Ireland and the United States."

"His visit comes during a remarkable sporting summer for Ireland, and the United States and this weekend's Irish Open at Trump International Doonbeg will be a fitting conclusion to an outstanding season of sport, and I hope we will see an Irish winner lifting the trophy on Sunday."

An avid golf fan, in July Trump said he hoped to travel to Doonbeg to watch the Irish Open.

In a special video message, he told the US Embassy's Fourth of July celebration event that he wants to see "Rory [McIlroy] and all the great players".

"There's nothing better than Irish-American friendship and I have a beautiful place over there - it's one of the best, most beautiful golf courses anywhere in the world," said Trump in his message, which was broadcast on a large screen.

"We have a place that's so top and we have the Irish Open going to be there.

"They call it Trump National, we sometimes use the name of the location, but it's Trump National Golf Club, and we're looking forward to it.

"We're going to have a tremendous celebration. I think I'm going to come over and I'm going to see it and watch. It'll be something very, very special."

President Connolly, an outspoken Gaza activist who has been critical of the US and said Trump is acting "like a bully" over tariffs, has come under pressure to raise issues in the Middle East during her brief meeting with the US president.

Sinn Féin and a series of other parties in the Republic who backed her in the Irish presidency campaign last year have called on her to raise Gaza during her meeting with Trump.

Ireland is one of the most pro-Palestinian countries in the European Union and has been criticised for its stance by Israel.

articles.title: 30% of college students say violence acceptable way to stop speakers on campuses, survey finds
articles.summary: The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression survey finds 30% of students find violence acceptable to stop speakers, one year after Charlie Kirk's assasination.
articles.body: Thirty percent of college students nationwide believe using violence is an acceptable way to stop a controversial speaker at a campus event, according to a new survey from the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE). Specifically, 3% said it was always acceptable, 12% said it was sometimes acceptable and 16% said it was rarely acceptable to use violence as a means of prohibiting a speaker from appearing on a college campus, according to FIRE's survey. The data comes a year after Charlie Kirk was assassinated during a college event held by his organization, Turning Point USA, on Sept. 10, 2025, while Kirk was engaging in debate with students. I’M A UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT. OUR PROFESSION SHOULD FINISH WHAT CHARLIE KIRK STARTED FIRE noted in its findings that the percentage has declined from last year. In 2025, 34% of students believed using violence as a protest action was acceptable. However, this year's findings are up 10 points from four years ago, according to FIRE. Seventy percent of students nationwide said in this year's findings that using violence was never acceptable to oppose a speaker. Similarly, 69% of students nationwide believe shouting down a speaker is acceptable, which is down three points from last year. However, the 2026 findings are still up seven points from four years ago. ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION FIRE Data Analyst Chapin Lenthall-Cleary told Fox News Digital in a statement, "We’re pleased that the percentage of students who find it acceptable to answer speech with violence has decreased. But so long as students and outside speakers believe that voicing disagreement or sharing controversial views could get them hurt, speech will remain chilled on campuses." Lenthall-Cleary said FIRE wasn't sure what caused a decline in this year's results with regard to acceptable responses to speakers on campus. "It's possible that students who once believed violence was an acceptable way to stop a campus speech changed their minds after witnessing Charlie Kirk get brutally assassinated for speaking his mind on a campus," he added. "Back in the early 2020s, when we started doing the rankings, liberal students were about twice as accepting of violence as conservative students. Since then, there's been a dramatic rise in acceptance of violence among conservative and moderate students, especially male students. JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS "Now, liberal and conservative students are roughly equally accepting of violence. Mercifully, overall support for violence declined slightly this year, but over 30% of students still say it's at least rarely acceptable to use violence to stop a speaker." Kirk was assassinated on the campus of Utah Valley University's campus. FIRE's survey found that the assassination had a lasting effect, both negative and positive, on free speech on UVU's campus. CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS The organization's rankings also include a comprehensive list of where colleges rank with regard to free speech and expression. FIRE's findings are based on surveys of 62,997 undergraduate students enrolled in four-year degree programs at 262 colleges and universities. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP According to the 2027 College Free Speech Rankings report, the top five schools for free speech are the University of Chicago, Claremont McKenna College, the Georgia Institute of Technology, Michigan Technological University and Vanderbilt University.

articles.title: Anti-migrant activists like Danny Tommo are changing tactics
articles.summary: Patriot Platform wants to build a group of working-class voters to influence political parties on the right.
articles.body:
At around seven o'clock last Saturday morning, dozens of men dressed in black climbed into the backs of lorries in a quiet Kent village called Preston-next-Wingham.

The men had arrived under cover of darkness the night before, leaving their cars everywhere: in the village hall car park and on the recreation ground.

In an operation with a degree of military precision, the small fleet of lorries departed for Dover just after sunrise, where the men staged an intimidating show of strength near the port.

In disciplined, serried ranks, they wore paramilitary-style balaclavas as they blocked roads around the port. There were at least three waves of arrivals, including the men who had spent the night in Preston-next-Wingham. Glaring ominously at motorists and police officers, they stood their ground.

Hardened anti-immigration campaigners were using their newly developed tactics for the first time.

It bore little resemblance to the running battles seen in cities in the Midlands in the days of Tommy Robinson's original vehicle, the anti-Muslim English Defence League (EDL).

"I seriously thought we'd been invaded by Russians," a Dover resident, Robin Burkhardt, told the BBC.

The main organiser Danny Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, said on Instagram afterwards: "This is our warning."

The style of protest is a new development in the crowded world of British hard-right and far-right politics. It was visually striking, and the men - who were part of a new group called Patriot Platform - chanted "Christ is King" as well as "Stop the Boats".

On Sunday, using a social media live stream, Thomas was able to organise a second, more impromptu protest of a few hundred people in his home city of Portsmouth.

His activists tried to block coaches that had come to collect migrants, who had arrived illegally, brought ashore after making the long journey from Normany in France.

On Thursday, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met senior police officers and urged them to make full use of their powers to stop activists wearing face coverings.

"These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," she said.

"This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."

Some of Patriot Platform's disruptive, eye-catching tactics seem to have been borrowed from environmental groups like Just Stop Oil. But its leaders are also getting ideas and funding from the growing "Christian nationalism" seen in the United States.

It organisers say they are building a working-class "voting bloc" to persuade political parties on the right to adopt their agenda.

The website for Patriot Platform was registered on 18 May this year, two days after a big anti-immigration "Unite the Kingdom" march in London.

Thomas, its most visible founder, first posted about the group on YouTube on 8 June.

"We need to be a bit smarter," he said, referencing arrests or offences including the assaults on police officers and violent disorder during recent Unite the Kingdom marches, that had been organised by Robinson. "Good men and women are now away from the fight stuck in jail cells."

Thomas told his supporters he had a few ideas that would be "more powerful than committing acts of violence and criminal damage".

There needs to be a "different MO", he said. "We are looking for the strong, the able, the ones that are willing to do things a bit different."

What sets Patriot Platform apart is the scale and co-ordination of their action, says William Allchorn of Anglia Ruskin University, an expert on far-right movements.

"There hasn't [previously] been co-ordinated mass activism with hundreds of people descending and trying to take matters, as it were, into their own hands," he says.

Thomas spent the summer posting further videos about the group and staging meetings in the North West, Essex, Leicester and Kent. He said he was trying to organise a "mass resistance" movement.

What happened in Dover demonstrated some of his new ways of working. The protesters were almost exclusively male. They arrived in well-organised waves in the backs of lorries. They did not engage with the media, and said little to members of the public whose journeys and weekends they were disrupting.

Then, after a few hours, before the police could get organised, the men all marched off to Dover Priory Station and left. Estimates vary as to how many were there but it looks like between 200 and 500.

The anti-racism group Hope Not Hate said Patriot Platform should be seen "for what it is: a far-right network of men happy to intimidate and inconvenience an entire town for what was effectively a publicity stunt".

Nick Lowles, the group's CEO, said Thomas had "been upfront about his intention to create a 'patriotic army that is able to take control of the United Kingdom'".

At a protest outside the Daily Mail offices in London on Wednesday, Thomas could be seen giving clear instructions to his supporters about his preferred tactics.

"Don't intimidate anyone," he ordered. "No one talk. Keep a distance. Five metres away from police".

Patriot Platform is coming into a crowded space of activists campaigning against immigration. Robinson's is the most high-profile brand. A former close associate of Danny Thomas, Robinson (whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon) has given Patriot Platform public support since Saturday.

But there is also Paul Golding's Britain First, Turning Point UK and the neo-Nazi Patriotic Alternative.

Thomas was once close to Ryan Bridge, the founder of a group called Raise the Colours, who have put up flags in towns across England over the last year.

But the pair have since publicly fallen out, with Thomas telling Bridge in an online rant: "Do I need to stab you in the eye?"

Thomas was jailed for two years in 2016 after he and two others tried to kidnap a man at knifepoint in Portsmouth in a dispute over money linked to drugs.

What seems to be different about Patriot Platform's approach now is that Thomas is explicitly talking about creating a "voting bloc" of supporters to back a yet-to-be decided party, which offers policies closest to what he wants, at the next general election.

"I do not support any political party at this moment in time," he said, adding that once the bloc was established, it would be made "extremely clear" which way the group's vote would go.

It's not clear whether Reform UK would get his backing. In a public confrontation with Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf in Portsmouth on Monday, Thomas complained that Nigel Farage had branded his Dover protest "disgusting".

"The working class do not vote," Thomas said. "We are going to make it a fashionable thing to take all your family members to the voting booth.

"But if your leader keeps slandering people, it's going to push them to other parties."

Waiting in the wings is the new party Restore Britain, launched by Rupert Lowe after he was suspended from Reform UK. On X, the party said it "stands with the patriots peacefully protesting against the invasion".

It is not clear how much support Thomas has. Parties like Reform and Restore will be very aware of the potential power that activists like Thomas and Robinson can now wield with their large social media followings. On X, Robinson has two million followers to Farage's 2.3 million, while Thomas has almost 163,000.

At Wednesday's protest, Thomas offered to pay supporters for any work they had missed to be there - in cash.

This kind of generosity might help explain why his activism - and that of his some-time mentor Robinson - have such a strong Christian message now. The Christian right in America can be a good source of funds.

Christianity is now a big part of Danny Thomas's brand. His calls for action are peppered with the occasional "Amen", pronounced in the American way, with the first syllable said "ay" rather than "ah".

He was pictured at St Lawrence church in south London in February and March.

The local diocese told BBC News that while it welcomed "people of various political and ideological perspectives", it remained "committed to the inclusion of all people" and the focus of worship would "always be the person of Christ, who is for everyone".

Thomas has spoken publicly about his new-found faith: "I have repented my sins and, under Jesus Christ, I am a new man."

Thomas is trying to raise money for Patriot Platform through a popular American Christian crowdfunding platform. Just below the "Give" and "Share" buttons, there is a "Pray" button.

On the page, Thomas says he is trying to raise £5,000 a month to pay for the likes of transport, boats and a studio. This month alone he has raised around £9,000.

This attempt to build Christianity into the brand is potentially also a way of painting the UK as a Christian country, and Muslim immigrants as outsiders.

As for what comes next for the Patriot Platform after its initial surge in supporters, far-right expert Allchorn thinks it's an unclear picture.

"A lot of these groups don't really have an end goal in mind," he says. "This often comes kind of later on when they are kind of forced to to come up with more concrete proposals and goals."

articles.title: UN extends partial Sudan arms embargo for a month
articles.summary: Sudan’s UN ambassador said a total arms embargo goes against the UN Charter that guarantees a right to self-defence.
articles.body:
The UN Security Council voted unanimously to briefly extend the arms embargo on Sudan’s western Darfur region while negotiations continue on a contentious US proposal to impose a nationwide ban.

All 15 Security Council members on Friday voted in favour of the one-month extension, which maintains the existing measures while allowing more time for negotiations on potential changes to the sanctions regime.

US Ambassador Jeff Bartos said Washington welcomed the adoption. “The current sanctions regime is over 20 years outdated, and is insufficient to address the realities of the war today,” he told the Security Council.

The US is proposing to expand the embargo throughout Sudan to pressure the warring parties to end their more than three-year conflict.

Bartos urged the council to “expand the arms embargo across the entire territory of Sudan, expand the listing measures to include horrific actions such as conflict-related sexual violence, kidnapping for ransom, and attacks on humanitarian personnel, and strengthen the mandate and effectiveness of the panel of experts.”

The Security Council imposed an arms embargo on the vast Darfur region after violence erupted in 2003 when rebels took up arms against the government in Khartoum, then led by Omar al-Bashir.

The government responded with air attacks and a ground offensive by government-linked militias called the Popular Defence Forces, known by the rebels as “Janjaweed”, who are accused of mass killings and rapes. Up to 300,000 people died in the conflict, and 2.7 million fled their homes.

Russia, which holds veto power in the council and backs the Sudanese government in its fight against paramilitary forces, pledged to prevent any expansion of the arms embargo.

Moscow made its “red lines” clear during closed negotiations, Russia’s deputy UN ambassador Anna Evstigneeva said Friday. “We will not allow even a hint of broadening the restrictions by the council on Sudan.”

Evstigneeva asked why the US was trying to expand the arms embargo now when government forces “have a definite advantage on the ground,” and not in 2023 when the RSF was threatening the capital, Khartoum, and other cities.

Sudan’s UN Ambassador Al-Harith Mohamed told the council that a total arms embargo goes against the UN Charter’s guarantee that countries have the right to self-defence and their armed forces have the right to produce and acquire weapons to protect their sovereignty.

At a council meeting on August 24, the US urged a countrywide arms embargo to push the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces to negotiate an end to fighting that began in April 2023.

The current war has killed at least 59,000 people, though aid groups warn the number could be much higher. It has displaced some 13 million people and pushed parts of the country into famine, creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

articles.title: North Korea launches ballistic missiles toward the sea following military drill it sees as threat
articles.summary: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea launched ballistic missiles toward the sea on Saturday, its neighbors said, a day after the U.S., South Korea and Japan ended their trilateral military drill that North Korea views as a security threat.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea launched ballistic missiles toward the sea on Saturday, its neighbors said, a day after the U.S., South Korea and Japan ended their trilateral military drill that North Korea views as a security threat. South Korea’s military said it detected the launches of several missiles from North Korea’s eastern costal Wonsan area. It said South Korea has boosted its surveillance posture and was closely exchanging information on the launches with the U.S. and Japan. The U.S. Pacific Command said the North’s launch event does not pose an immediate threat to U.S. territory or to its allies. It said the U.S. remains committed to the defense of the U.S. homeland and our allies in the region. South Korea’s military said the five-day Freedom Edge exercise is defensive in nature and meant to enhance a joint response capability against North Korean nuclear threats. Hours after the drill began Monday, North Korea’s defense minister, Kim Song Gi, criticized the exercise and warned North Korea was capable of taking “strong and reflective countermeasures from the standpoint of power.”

articles.title: Board votes to rename Nashville International Airport for Dolly Parton
articles.summary: Nashville’s airport authority board unanimously voted Friday to begin the process to rename the city’s airport to honor late country music legend and Tennessee icon Dolly Parton.
articles.body: Nashville’s airport authority board unanimously voted Friday to begin the process to rename the city’s airport to honor late country music legend and Tennessee icon Dolly Parton. The vote by the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority did not establish a new name for Nashville International Airport, but it begins the process, the board said in a statement. “It’s official!” Nashville International Airport said on social media when announcing the 6-0 airport authority vote, which the board described as “the first step in a multifaceted process.” Parton, beloved by country music fans around the world, died last month at the age of 80 after a brief battle with cancer, her family said on Aug. 25. “While a final name has not yet been determined, we are working closely with the appropriate parties to thoughtfully determine how Dolly Parton’s name and legacy will be incorporated,” the airport authority said. The airport authority said that it anticipates having more definitive plans to share about the implementation in the coming months. “We are grateful for the tremendous support and enthusiasm from our community and Dolly’s fans around the world,” it said. “We look forward to sharing additional details as plans are finalized. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee thanked the airport authority board for its action Friday and called the vote an “important step to honor her remarkable legacy.” “Dolly has always helped the world fall in love with Tennessee,” he said.

articles.title: UK weather: Is a September heatwave on the way?
articles.summary: Temperatures will return to summerlike levels over the weekend, despite some heavy rain.
articles.body:
Temperatures are set to climb across the UK this weekend, reaching summerlike levels in some places.

It will feel warm and muggy - especially where there are sunny spells - although heavy rain also features in the forecast.

The warmth will persist into Monday in many areas but nowhere is expected to reach heatwave criteria and cooler conditions are due to return by midweek.

Computer weather models paint a very mixed picture for the second half of September but, while there are likely to be some warm spells, there are currently no definitive signs of a heatwave.

Outbreaks of rain will spread southwards during Saturday, clearing from Scotland and Northern Ireland but continuing into the afternoon across parts of northern England, Wales and the Midlands.

Some of the rain could be heavy with a chance of thunder and lightning and will be accompanied by brisk south-westerly winds.

Southern parts of England should stay largely dry with sunny intervals and it will feel particularly warm and humid with temperatures climbing into the mid-20s Celsius - several degrees above the September average.

On Sunday, rain may linger for a while in southern England but should clear to leave a dry afternoon for much of the UK with sunny spells and light winds.

Temperatures may drop slightly in the northern half of the country but rise a little further south. Parts of Wales, the Midlands and southern England could reach 23-25C.

Monday could be even warmer with highs of 22-26C across much of England and Wales, and 20C likely in parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland.

However, while this will undoubtedly feel warm, it will remain below the criteria for a heatwave.

This would require three consecutive days of temperatures above a threshold which varies from 25C in Scotland and Northern Ireland to 28C in the London area.

Is there hot weather in the long-range forecast?

Computer models currently suggest unsettled weather will continue over the next week or so.

The jet stream is expected to bring areas of low pressure across the UK - meaning spells of rain and, potentially, some rather blustery winds.

The prospect of wet weather will be welcome for the large swathes of England and Wales that remain in drought.

Later in the month, areas of high pressure may have more influence on the weather which would mean longer dry interludes and the chance of above-average daytime temperatures.

While long-range forecasting is fraught with uncertainty and details are subject to change, there is currently nothing to indicate that a heatwave is on the cards.

Indeed, as autumn advances and the nights become longer, high pressure overhead could lead to some rather chilly mornings.

You can keep an eye on the temperatures where you are by checking BBC Weather online and the app .

articles.title: Former top US diplomat reveals mistakes made after 9/11 attacks
articles.summary: Ambassador Zalmay Khalilzad describes misgivings about the US handling of the Afghanistan and Iraq wars.
articles.body:
Twenty-five years after the attacks on September 11, 2001, a former top United States diplomat has outlined what he feels were missteps made in the aftermath.

In an interview on Friday with journalist Alex Marquardt for the Al Jazeera programme This is America , Ambassador Zalmay Khalilzad described how the country’s heightened sense of fear led to a series of spiralling decisions that would transform the world for years to come.

“Anger was a factor of urgency because the people wanted to see action: What are we going to do about this?” Khalilzad said of the attacks.

The events of September 11 are considered the deadliest foreign attack in US history. Nearly 3,000 people died when 19 hijackers crashed passenger jets into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania.

Less than a month after the attacks, the US launched an invasion of Afghanistan, with the stated aim of attacking the group responsible, al-Qaeda. It was the start of a nearly 20-year-long war.

“You have to put yourself in the context of the time. We were very angry. We were concerned that other attacks may be planned. There may be sleeper cells,” Khalilzad said. “We wanted to get to as many people – al-Qaeda members – to arrest them.”

Khalilzad was a senior director on the National Security Council at the time of the attacks, serving under then-President George W Bush.

He later served in several ambassadorships, representing the US as the top diplomat in Afghanistan, Iraq and the United Nations at various points in his career.

In Friday’s interview, he described having misgivings about US policy toward Afghanistan, including the decision not to negotiate with the Taliban, which ruled the country at the time of the invasion.

Reports have since emerged that the Taliban was willing to strike a deal with the US in 2001, in the early months of the war. But the US reportedly rejected the possibility of a deal.

The Taliban fought US-backed forces for the next two decades, until the US withdrawal in 2021. Since then, it has retaken power.

“One thought that has emerged is that we should have negotiated with the Taliban or included the Taliban in the political process in Afghanistan,” Khalilzad said. “It would have been good if that had happened.”

He credits the decision not to enter into negotiations to several factors, including post-September 11 anger and the US’s status as a global superpower.

“We were angry, and we wanted to get information from them,” Khalilzad said of the Taliban. “But if we could have included them … realistically, that could have been helpful.”

In 2003, two years after the Afghanistan invasion, the US launched a separate operation against Iraq as part of its growing so-called “war on terror”.

The Bush administration justified that war by citing now-infamous intelligence assessments that Iraq was on the verge of obtaining “weapons of mass destruction”, including nuclear capabilities. Those reports would later turn out to be false.

Still, the war in Iraq would last more than eight years and would result in the overthrow and execution of Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein.

“With regard to Iraq, well, there the information was the problem,” Khalilzad said, adding: “I think, in retrospect, the circumstances, the analysis, the information was problematic.”

At the time, Khalilzad said, the US did not believe Hussein had been truthful about whether his country possessed weapons of mass destruction. The US also feared another “surprise attack”, similar to what al-Qaeda had launched.

“Without 9/11, I don’t think we will attack Iraq,” Khalilzad said.

He explained that the US government believed that, if “this problem of Saddam Hussein is also allowed to percolate”, the country could “face a huge surprise and attack”.

“Containment evolved into massive attack and overthrowing of the regime,” Khalilzad said.

In August, the US marked five years since its chaotic military withdrawal from Afghanistan.

The process began in 2020, when President Donald Trump, during his first term, signed a deal with the Taliban to pull out all US troops by the following year. It was completed during the presidency of Joe Biden in 2021.

The withdrawal was widely criticised for putting troops at risk and leaving behind Afghans who had worked with US-allied forces and who were therefore at risk of violence and punishment.

For his part, Khalilzad said he agreed with the move to pull US troops from the country.

“We had been there for 20 years. Afghanistan was changed. The war could have gone on indefinitely. The world had changed. Priorities had changed. We decimated the terrorist threat. That’s what had driven us,” he said.

Shortly after US forces left the country, the US-backed Afghan government fell, and the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan.

But Khalilzad argued the new relationship has been positive for the US: “I think the Taliban, surprisingly, have been good in terms of terrorism for the United States interests.”
